lines.text: High in the Andes, between a sacred lake and a mountain of silver, a nation was forged. This is the story of Bolivia.
It begins with Lake Titicaca, formed perhaps two or three million years ago, one of the highest navigable lakes in the world.
On its shores, the people of Tiwanaku built a powerful state, with great stone monuments like the Gate of the Sun and fields raised high above the sea.
Centuries later the Incas spread along the Andes from Cusco and brought these highlands into their vast empire.
Then came Spain. In 1538 the Spanish founded the town that is now Sucre, the country's constitutional capital.
In 1545 silver was found, and Potosi became one of the largest and richest cities of its age.
Its wealth came from the Cerro Rico, the rich mountain, mined for centuries at a terrible cost to the Indigenous workers forced into it.
Three years later La Paz was founded, today the seat of government and the highest capital in the world.
Antonio Jose de Sucre was born in Venezuela. He would win the battle that ended Spanish rule in South America, and become Bolivia's first president.
In 1809 revolts broke out in Chuquisaca and La Paz, beginning a long war for independence.
Independence came in 1825, and the new country took its name from the liberator, Simon Bolivar.
Simon Patino was born. From Bolivian tin he would build one of the greatest fortunes of his time.
In the War of the Pacific, Chile took Bolivia's coastal deserts, and the country lost its access to the sea.
In Argentina, Che Guevara was born. Years later, after the Cuban revolution, he would come to Bolivia to spread revolt, and die there.
From 1932 Bolivia fought Paraguay over the Chaco, a bitter war that cost Bolivia more land.
In 1952 revolution came, bringing votes for all adults, land reform and the takeover of the great tin mines.
Evo Morales was born, a future coca growers' leader who would become Bolivia's first Indigenous president.
Rodrigo Paz was born, the man who decades later would be elected president of Bolivia.
In the south lies the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat on Earth, a vast white mirror after the rains.
In 2003 protests erupted over plans to export the country's gas, and they toppled governments.
In 2019, after a disputed election, mass protests forced Evo Morales to resign.
And in 2025 voters ended twenty years of rule by his party, the Movement for Socialism.
From Tiwanaku's stones to today's elections, Bolivia's story is still written high in the Andes.
